chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abdullah and someone else, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdullah, from his father, from Abdullah ibn al-Qasim, from a man from the people of Sabata, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to Ammar al-Sabati: 'O Ammar, you are a lord of much wealth?' He said, 'Yes, may I be sacrificed for you.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'So do you pay what Allah has imposed upon you from the Zakat?' He said, 'Yes.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'So you take out the known right from your wealth?' He said, 'Yes.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'So you connect with your relatives?' He said, 'Yes.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'And you connect with your brothers?' He said, 'Yes.' So he (peace be upon him) said: 'O Ammar, indeed wealth perishes and the body wears out, and the deed remains, and the Judge is Living and will not die. O Ammar, whatever you send forward, it will not precede you, and whatever you delay, it will not join you.'
ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) teach about the permanence of deeds versus wealth?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi highlights the practical application of wealth management in Shia jurisprudence, specifically linking Zakat, Khums, and Silat al-Rahim as essential components of spiritual preservation. Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) uses Ammar al-Sabati, a known companion and merchant, to illustrate that while material assets and the physical body are perishable, righteous deeds endure with the Ever-Living Judge (Al-Hayy Al-Qayyum). The narration underscores the transient nature of worldly wealth compared to the permanence of one's moral and spiritual legacy in the Hereafter.
